passage:
Monday. Aadhya lit a sandalwood incense stick in their hostel room. Within a minute Ira was snapping about the mess on the desk, jaw tight. Aadhya blew the stick out. Ira's shoulders dropped, though she didn't seem to notice why.
Thursday. It happened again in the corridor when someone else burned the same kind. Ira went rigid and said, "Can we go out?" Aadhya just said, "Sure," and didn't ask.
Two weeks later. Folding laundry, Aadhya said lightly, "I've noticed sandalwood seems to bother you. I'll keep it out of the room. You don't have to explain."
Ira looked up for a long moment. "Thanks. I honestly don't know why it does."

qa.q: What kind of incense did Aadhya light?
qa.a: A sandalwood incense stick.

qa.q: What does Ira's 'I honestly don't know why it does' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the reaction comes from something Ira can't reach or put into words, so the irritation feels real to her but has no clear reason.

qa.q: Which choice of Aadhya's worked, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya named the pattern kindly and kept sandalwood out without asking for a story, which let Ira feel safe instead of questioned.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ira to have a roommate who doesn't ask?
qa.a: It probably feels like relief; Ira gets understanding without having to explain something even she can't explain.

grounding: Over two weeks a hostel roommate notices a friend turn rigid and irritable at sandalwood and responds kindly without digging for a reason.

passage:
Charu, you asked how to live with a roommate you don't fully understand. When I was nineteen, in the women's hostel in Pune, I shared a room with Meenal. Lovely girl. But if anyone said, "Don't make a scene," even as a joke, she went stiff as a board and snapped at whoever spoke next.
I wanted to know why. Oh, how I wanted to know! But I only said to her once, quietly, "That phrase seems to upset you. I won't use it." She said, "I can't tell you why." I said, "You don't have to."
We shared that room for three years. She never told me, and I never asked again. At my wedding, Meenal was the first to arrive.
Your Rekha aunty has learnt a few things, you see.

qa.q: What phrase made Meenal go stiff?
qa.a: "Don't make a scene."

qa.q: Why did young Rekha want so badly to know the reason?
qa.a: Rekha was curious and probably wanted to help, but she chose to put Meenal's comfort ahead of her own need to understand.

qa.q: What choice did Rekha make that kept the friendship strong?
qa.a: Naming the reaction kindly once, promising not to use the phrase, and never digging for a story Meenal hadn't offered.

qa.q: What might Meenal arriving first at the wedding say about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Meenal felt deeply respected by Rekha's restraint, and that the friendship meant a great deal to her.

grounding: An older woman recalls how, as a student, she noticed a roommate's sharp reaction to a phrase and respected it without asking why.

passage:
The power had gone out at ten, the night before their final exam, and the two roommates were studying by one rechargeable lamp in their tiny Hyderabad flat. Jatin, frazzled, muttered, "Useless, useless," at his own notes.
Across the table Ramesh went rigid. "Can you not say that word," he said sharply, and shoved his chair back so hard it scraped.
Jatin stared. Ramesh never snapped. There was no time for a long talk and no other room to escape to. So Jatin said, "Sorry. I'll drop it," and turned the lamp a little toward Ramesh's side.
After a while Ramesh said, "I don't even know why it gets to me."
"You don't have to know," Jatin said. "Pass the highlighter?"

qa.q: What word did Jatin mutter at his notes?
qa.a: Useless.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when Ramesh snapped about the word?
qa.a: Jatin was startled, since Ramesh never snapped, but stayed calm and caring, saying sorry and turning the lamp toward Ramesh's side.

qa.q: What choice did Jatin make under exam pressure, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jatin apologised, dropped the word and turned the lamp toward Ramesh without asking for a story, keeping the night calm and Ramesh's privacy intact.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel when Jatin says 'You don't have to know'?
qa.a: Ramesh probably feels relieved not to be pushed for an explanation he doesn't have, and accepted anyway.

grounding: During a power cut before an exam, a roommate sees his friend react sharply to one word and kindly lets it be without probing.

passage: In their Bengaluru PG room, Uma noticed it for the third time on Thursday. Their friend Gauri, visiting, teased Jaya about the messy desk: "Are you deaf? I called you three times!" She laughed as she said it. Jaya went rigid, cheeks tight, and snapped, "Don't talk to me like that," then walked out. Gauri stared, hurt. "It was a joke!" Uma had seen the same thing twice before, at exactly those words. Jaya herself had once said, puzzled, "I don't know why that line makes me so angry." Uma didn't chase her or ask what had happened in the past. Later, bringing two cups of tea to the balcony, she said, "I noticed that phrase really gets to you. You don't have to explain. Want me to tell Gauri quietly to skip it?" Jaya let out a breath. "Yes. Thanks."

qa.q: What phrase did Gauri say to Jaya?
qa.a: "Are you deaf? I called you three times!"

qa.q: What might Jaya have felt, going rigid and snapping at Gauri?
qa.a: A strong, sudden anger came up at those exact words, and even Jaya didn't know why, which made the reaction confusing for Jaya too.

qa.q: What did Uma choose not to do, and why was that wise?
qa.a: Uma didn't dig for a story from Jaya's past, which respected Jaya's privacy and still offered practical help.

qa.q: How might Gauri see Jaya's reaction to a joke?
qa.a: Gauri felt hurt and confused, seeing only an angry reply to something meant playfully.

grounding: A roommate notices her friend's strong reaction to a phrase and kindly acknowledges it without digging for an explanation.

passage: "Siddharth, did you buy a new floor cleaner?" "Yeah, the strong one. Why?" "It smells like... I don't know. I hate it." "It's just phenyl, Pradeep." "Can you open the window?" "It's raining." "Just open it!" "Okay, okay." "Sorry. I didn't mean to shout." "Bhai, you've gone all stiff. Your hands." "I don't know why. It's a smell. It's stupid." "It's not stupid. Some smells just hit people." "You're not going to ask what it's about?" "Not unless you want to tell me. I'll just get the other cleaner next time." "...Thanks." "Want to sit on the balcony till it clears?" "Yeah." They sat side by side under the dripping edge of the roof, not talking, and watched the rain on the road.

qa.q: What kind of floor cleaner had Siddharth bought?
qa.a: The strong one; phenyl.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he asked Siddharth to open the window and then apologised?
qa.a: He felt a sudden, strong discomfort at the smell that he couldn't explain, then felt bad for shouting at his friend.

qa.q: Which of Siddharth's choices helped Pradeep most?
qa.a: Not pushing for a reason, saying it wasn't stupid, and offering to switch cleaners and sit on the balcony together.

qa.q: What might it mean to Pradeep that Siddharth didn't ask what the smell was about?
qa.a: It is likely a relief for Pradeep not to have to explain something with no words for it yet, and it makes sitting together on the balcony feel safe.

grounding: A flatmate sees a friend react strongly to a smell without knowing why, and responds kindly without digging for a story.
